description: Individual needs, specificity, progressive overload, FITT and training thresholds explained.
content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Elite athletes do not train randomly. Their programmes are built on scientific principles that ensure each session produces the right adaptations without causing injury, boredom or wasted effort. Understanding these principles is essential for designing, evaluating and improving any training programme — whether for a school athlete, a club-level performer or a professional.

Individual Needs and Specificity

The first step in any programme is to assess the athlete’s individual needs. Individual needs recognises that no two athletes are the same. Age, fitness level, previous training history, current health status and the demands of the sport all vary. A 16-year-old beginner runner needs a very different programme from an experienced county-level distance runner of the same age.

Specificity means that training must replicate the demands of the sport. A sprinter must develop fast-twitch muscle fibres and the anaerobic energy system through short, explosive efforts — long, slow jogging would not produce the right adaptations. A swimmer must train in the water to develop sport-specific muscle recruitment patterns and technique under fatigue. If training is not specific, fitness gains will not transfer to improved performance.

Progressive Overload

Progressive overload states that the body only adapts when it is challenged beyond its current capacity. A load that was challenging four weeks ago will no longer produce adaptation once the body has adjusted to it. To continue improving, the athlete must progressively increase the training stimulus. This can be achieved by increasing frequency (training more days per week), intensity (working at a higher percentage of maximum heart rate or one rep max), time (training for longer durations) or type (introducing new and more demanding training methods). These four variables form the FITT framework.

Key Fact

FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), Type (what method). All four variables can be manipulated to create progressive overload. For example, a runner could increase frequency from 3 to 4 sessions per week (frequency), run at 75% rather than 65% of maximum heart rate (intensity), extend sessions from 30 to 40 minutes (time), or add interval training alongside continuous runs (type).

Reversibility and Overtraining

Reversibility — sometimes called detraining — describes the loss of fitness adaptations when training stops. Cardiovascular fitness declines within 2–3 weeks of stopping aerobic training; muscular adaptations take longer to reverse but will decline with inactivity. Injury, illness and competition breaks all present reversibility risks. Athletes must plan rest carefully to avoid detraining while allowing recovery.

Overtraining is the opposite danger: pushing the body too hard without sufficient rest. Symptoms include persistent fatigue, declining performance, increased injury risk, mood changes and suppressed immune function. A well-designed programme builds overload gradually and includes planned rest and recovery phases.

Training Thresholds and Heart Rate Zones

To ensure training intensity is at the right level, coaches use training thresholds based on percentages of maximum heart rate. Maximum heart rate is estimated using the formula: maximum heart rate = 220 − age. For a 16-year-old, this gives 220 − 16 = 204 beats per minute (bpm).

The aerobic training zone sits between 60% and 80% of maximum heart rate. For a 16-year-old (max HR 204 bpm): lower boundary = 0.60 × 204 = 122 bpm; upper boundary = 0.80 × 204 = 163 bpm. Training within this zone develops cardiovascular endurance because the body is using oxygen efficiently to sustain effort.

The anaerobic training zone sits between 80% and 90% of maximum heart rate. For the same 16-year-old: lower boundary = 0.80 × 204 = 163 bpm; upper boundary = 0.90 × 204 = 184 bpm. At this intensity, the body cannot supply oxygen fast enough, so anaerobic pathways are used. Lactic acid accumulates, which limits duration. This zone develops speed, power and the ability to tolerate high-intensity effort.

Key Fact

Max HR formula: 220 − age. Aerobic zone: 60–80% of max HR (predominantly oxygen-based, builds cardiovascular endurance). Anaerobic zone: 80–90% of max HR (oxygen insufficient, builds speed/power, lactic acid produced). The boundaries are calculated by multiplying max HR by the decimal percentage.

A SMART target is a goal that is Specific (names the exact skill or component), Measurable (has a number), Achievable (within the athlete’s capacity), Realistic (appropriate to their current level) and Time-bound (has a deadline). A poorly written target is “I want to get better at running.” A well-written SMART target is: “I will improve my Cooper 12-minute run distance from 2,100 m to 2,300 m within 8 weeks of following my aerobic training programme.” This target names the test (specific and measurable), the improvement is within reach (achievable and realistic) and it has a deadline (time-bound). Mark schemes credit only targets that satisfy all five criteria simultaneously.

Students sometimes write that “progressive overload means working harder every session.” This risks overtraining. In reality, well-designed programmes build load progressively over several weeks, then include a ‘recovery week’ where volume drops before the next loading block begins. The key is that overload is introduced gradually and systematically over time, not relentlessly session by session. The body adapts during rest and recovery, not during the training stimulus itself — without adequate rest, the adaptations cannot occur and performance will stagnate or decline.
exam_tip_html: On Calculate questions involving training zones, always show three steps: (1) calculate max HR using 220 − age, (2) multiply max HR by the lower boundary percentage, (3) multiply max HR by the upper boundary percentage. Show the units (bpm) at each step. A common error is to apply the percentage directly to 220 rather than to the calculated max HR — this will give a wrong answer. For Explain questions on SMART targets, examiners expect all five criteria to be referenced, not just one or two. Write the target out in full and annotate which element satisfies each letter.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Effective training programmes apply individual needs (tailored to the athlete), specificity (matches sport demands), progressive overload (gradually increasing load), and FITT (manipulating frequency, intensity, time and type) to drive adaptation.
  • Reversibility means fitness is lost without training; overtraining means too much load without rest. Both must be avoided through careful programme design.
  • Training zones are calculated from max HR (220 − age): aerobic zone = 60–80% of max HR; anaerobic zone = 80–90% of max HR. These guide intensity for cardiovascular training.

practice_questions.text:
Which principle of training states that fitness adaptations will be lost if training stops?
A) Specificity
B) Progressive overload
C) Reversibility
D) Individual needs
A 15-year-old sprinter has a maximum heart rate of 205 bpm. Calculate the lower boundary of her anaerobic training zone.
practice_questions.marks: Working: 0.80 x 205 = 164 bpm (1 mark for correct calculation); 164 bpm (1 mark for correct answer with units). Accept calculation shown as 80/100 x 205.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'specificity' as a principle of training and give one example of it applied to a sport.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: specificity means training must match the specific demands of the sport (1); targeting the relevant muscles, energy systems and movement patterns used in that sport (1); example — a swimmer trains primarily in the water to develop the specific muscle recruitment and cardiovascular adaptations needed for competitive swimming (1). Accept other valid sporting examples.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the FITT principle can be applied to create progressive overload in a training programme for a 16-year-old club-level cyclist.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks, one for each FITT variable applied to cycling: Frequency — increase from 3 to 4 training rides per week (1); Intensity — increase from 65% to 75% of max HR during rides (1); Time — extend each ride from 45 minutes to 60 minutes (1); Type — add interval sessions alongside steady-state rides (1). Award up to 3 marks total.

practice_questions.text: A county-level 14-year-old distance runner is designing a 10-week training programme. Analyse how applying the principles of training would help her optimise her programme.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Individual needs: assesses current fitness level (e.g. Cooper run test result) to identify starting point. Specificity: training focuses on cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance needed for distance running, using running-based sessions. Progressive overload via FITT: gradually increases weekly mileage (time/frequency), raises intensity from aerobic to the upper aerobic zone over weeks, varies type (long runs, tempo runs). Reversibility awareness: includes planned rest days and a recovery week at week 5 to allow adaptation without detraining. SMART target set for the 10-week endpoint (e.g. improve Cooper run score). All principles linked explicitly to distance running performance. Technically accurate.

Secure: Applies three or more principles correctly with running application. Mostly accurate.

Developing: Names principles without full application. Some running context.

Emerging: Names one principle. Minimal application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether progressive overload or specificity is the more important principle when designing a training programme for a competitive 16-year-old middle-distance runner.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For specificity — if training does not match the demands of middle-distance running (aerobic and anaerobic systems, muscular endurance of the legs, running technique), fitness gains will not transfer to performance; a non-specific programme (e.g. cycling only) would not develop running economy or race-pace tolerance. For progressive overload — without systematic increase in training load, the body plateaus; specificity of content is worthless if the stimulus never exceeds current capacity. Conclusion: both are essential and interdependent; specificity defines what to train, overload defines how to progress it. A programme that is specific but stagnant will not improve performance; one that overloads but is not specific will improve general fitness but not competitive times. Balanced, applied to middle-distance running, concluded.

Secure: Addresses both principles with running application. Reaches a conclusion. Mostly accurate.

Developing: Focuses on one principle more. Some sporting application.

Emerging: Describes one principle. No comparative evaluation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does specificity mean as a training principle?
flashcard_questions.a: Training must match the specific muscles, energy systems and movements demanded by the sport.
Training load must be gradually increased over time to continue producing fitness adaptations.

flashcard_questions.q: What does reversibility mean in training?
flashcard_questions.a: Fitness adaptations are lost if training stops or is significantly reduced.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the acronym FITT stand for?
What is the formula for estimating maximum heart rate?
What percentage range defines the aerobic training zone?
What percentage range defines the anaerobic training zone?

flashcard_questions.a: A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound.
Declining performance, fatigue, increased injury risk and suppressed immune function.

flashcard_questions.q: What does individual needs mean as a training principle?
flashcard_questions.a: Training must be tailored to the specific fitness level, age, sport and goals of the individual athlete.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the body need rest as part of a training programme?
flashcard_questions.a: Adaptations occur during recovery, not during the training stimulus itself.

flashcard_questions.q: Calculate the upper boundary of the aerobic training zone for a 16-year-old athlete.
flashcard_questions.a: Max HR = 204 bpm; upper aerobic boundary = 0.80 x 204 = 163 bpm.

glossary_terms.definition: The principle that training must be tailored to the specific demands of the individual athlete, taking into account their current fitness levels, age, sport and goals.
The principle that training must match the specific demands of the sport, targeting the relevant muscles, energy systems and movement patterns.
The principle that training load must be gradually and systematically increased over time to continue producing fitness adaptations.
An acronym describing the four training variables that can be adjusted to create overload: Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type.
The principle that fitness adaptations are lost if training is stopped or significantly reduced over a period of time.
The negative state that results from training too hard, too frequently or without adequate rest, leading to declining performance, injury or illness.
The minimum intensity required for exercise to produce a training effect; working above this threshold causes fitness adaptations.
The heart rate range of 60-80% of maximum heart rate at which the aerobic energy system is primarily used, developing cardiovascular endurance.
The heart rate range of 80-90% of maximum heart rate at which the anaerobic energy system predominates, developing speed and power.
A framework for setting effective training goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound.
